NAME

md_docs_2transport-backpressure - Transport backpressure and media admission

Every native connection owns a plaintext outbound scheduler. Browser WebSocket, WebRTC and hosted peer sessions use the same contract through OutboundQueue. Backend event loops remain independent; none decides whether video is disposable.

Capacity and ownership

The hard per-connection accounted budget is 8 MiB. Video cannot use the final 1 MiB: 512 KiB is reserved for audio and another 512 KiB for control. Packet-count limits reserve descriptors too (448 video, 480 audio, 512 total). Accounting reserves plaintext, two wire/encryption owners, protocol overhead and descriptors. Native TCP/WebSocket request a 64 KiB socket send buffer and reserve 128 KiB within the budget, covering Linux socket accounting. Receive buffers retain their normal tuning. Native SCTP send space is capped and reserves 64 KiB within this budget, because libdatachannel does not expose that retained amount in buffered bytes. Both rtcSctpSettings.sendBufferSize and each peer's rtcConfiguration.maxMessageSize are set to that same 64 KiB limit: libdatachannel raises its SCTP socket buffer to at least the local maximum message size. Larger ACIP packets are split into negotiated-size DataChannel messages by the existing transport and reassembled before ACIP decoding. Snapshots report the fixed reservation separately from measured backend bytes. Backend pending bytes are additional; Receive buffers and bytes already in the network are outside this outbound budget.

Media submissions copy the borrowed plaintext before returning accepted. Expected congestion is a separate admission disposition, not a network failure. The public acip_outbound_submitv returns asciichat_error_t plus an acip_admission_t. Existing convenience send functions translate non-admission to ERROR_BUFFER_FULL; callers retain a usable connection and distinguish that from fatal write failure. Audio/control rejection is explicit. Already admitted reliable packets are never silently removed. A persistently blocked reliable queue closes the connection: five seconds for waiting audio, ten seconds for waiting control. A transport that has already accepted bytes remains responsible for its own failure/deadline handling.

One native worker serializes each connection's final write order. Handshake and setup/control calls (except ping/pong) wait until backend submission, preserving negotiation barriers. Enqueueing is serialized with admission and budget reservation. The caller must quiesce producers before destroying a transport, as with the existing transport lifetime contract. Destruction stops admission, interrupts writes, joins the worker, and releases every queued owner before backend resources are freed.

Scheduling and codec recovery

Independent raw image and ASCII snapshots replace older wholly unsent snapshots of the same stream. Video expires after 100 ms waiting in the application queue. Audio and ping/pong may precede unsent video, retaining FIFO order within their traffic classes and never crossing a setup/teardown/negotiation barrier. Other controls remain FIFO barriers. Encryption happens after these decisions. Neither ciphertext nor a partly submitted packet can be reordered, discarded, or retried.

Backends receive one complete ACIP packet at a time. Scheduling waits for reported pending bytes to drain before committing the next packet of any class. This keeps tiny control packets from building a long opaque FIFO behind video. Liveness pings/pongs enqueue asynchronously; setup and negotiation calls retain their synchronous submission barriers.

Bytes already in a socket, SCTP, or the network cannot be removed. A frame straddling a receiver throttle can therefore be older than 100 ms; that age is measured rather than hidden.

H.264 and H.265 share conservative dependency handling. After any queued encoded frame is discarded, all unsent pictures for that codec/stream are removed and subsequent dependent pictures are rejected until a keyframe is admitted. Native and browser capture request a fresh keyframe from their encoder. Native encoders request closed recovery pictures with repeated parameter sets. Browser WebCodecs continues its Annex B parameter-set handling. Discarding that recovery frame invalidates the stream again. Stream state is bounded to 64 codec/stream pairs.

acip_outbound_snapshot and browser snapshot() distinguish local admission, backend submission, drops, congestion, recovery frames, application/backend bytes, and oldest queued video age. Submission is not receiver delivery. Server logging now calls its counter admission FPS; the live harness measures receiver FPS.

Verification

Build ascii-chat, test-backpressure, test-backpressure-live, test-network-events, and test-webrtc-security. Run the deterministic test before the live matrix: 

build/bin/test-backpressure
uv run --project tests/ascii_chat_tests --frozen python -m pytest tests/python/integration/backpressure \


  --backpressure-probe build/bin/test-backpressure-live --backpressure-output build/backpressure

The live test opens real TCP, libwebsockets and libdatachannel connections. TCP and WebSocket throttle the receive path to 4 KiB every 64 ms for three seconds. WebSocket uses a bounded transparent TCP relay and an independent receiver service thread, preserving the production libwebsockets flow-control behavior after a two-second baseline. WebRTC advertises a UDP relay as its ICE candidate, verifies the selected remote port, and paces its datagrams during the same interval. A healthy connection runs alongside the saturated one. Each case restores capacity for ten seconds, verifies fresh frame and control delivery, then disconnects with queued data. Audio sequence checks verify ordering. For both encoded codecs, every keyframe starts a brand-new FFmpeg decoder; every delivered frame must decode successfully with no decoder corruption flags. Legal codec filler NAL units pad encoded packets to at least 16 KiB so encoder bitrate defaults cannot accidentally bypass saturation. Raw packets contain an 80x45 RGB image. Control pings are interleaved with every generated frame.

CSV records application/backend bytes, oldest queued video age, delivered count, drops, and the latest receiver-observed frame age. Logs and summary.json record peak queues, mean/max receiver frame age, delivered FPS by phase, healthy-peer FPS, control delivery, and codec recovery. Decoder delivery is measured here; terminal presentation is separately covered by network_fps_windows.py.

The Windows LGPL FFmpeg bundle may lack a working HEVC encoder. Use --backpressure-codecs raw,h264 there and run the full raw/H.264/H.265 matrix with a software HEVC-enabled FFmpeg build on Linux/macOS. An unavailable codec is a failed scenario in the runner, never silently counted as a pass.
